summary: Describes using AES counter mode, with an explicit initialization vector, as a confidentiality mechanism in IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Secret messages in IPsec can be scrambled many ways. This explains how to use AES counter mode for scrambling, which makes a stream of fresh scrambling values to mix into the message.

subtitle: How to encrypt IPsec packets with AES in counter mode, and the traps that make it unsafe if misused.

tldr.problem: IPsec ESP needs a confidentiality mechanism, and AES counter mode is attractive for fast networking but is easy to use in ways that destroy its security.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet carries an 8-octet IV. It is combined with a 32-bit nonce and a 32-bit block counter to form a 128-bit counter block, which AES encrypts to produce a key stream that is XORed with the data.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST use fresh keys (for example from IKE) and MUST pair AES-CTR with a non-NULL ESP authentication method. Never reuse an IV with the same key.

today: RFC 3686 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2004. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3686 describes how to use the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in counter mode (AES-CTR), with an explicit initialization vector (IV), as a confidentiality mechanism for the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). AES is a block cipher that can be used in several modes, and NIST has defined five of them: ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR. This document covers only CTR.

The RFC does not explain IPsec itself. It points readers to the IPsec architecture and roadmap documents for that.
sections.eli5: IPsec is a way to lock up internet traffic. This paper explains one specific kind of lock, built from the AES cipher in its counter mode.

sections.title: How AES Counter Mode Works
sections.content:
AES-CTR turns the AES block cipher into a stream cipher. The encryptor builds a sequence of counter blocks, encrypts each with AES to get 128 bits of key stream, and XORs the key stream with the plaintext. Decryption is the same XOR applied to the ciphertext. Because extra key stream bits are simply discarded, the plaintext does not need to be padded to a multiple of the block size, although padding MAY be included for limited traffic flow confidentiality.

The mode needs a unique per-packet value, which the RFC calls the IV. The same IV and key combination MUST NOT be used more than once. How the IV is generated is up to the encryptor, as long as it is unique. Incrementing a counter and linear feedback shift registers (LFSRs) are the common approaches.

The RFC lists the attractions for high-speed networking: AES-CTR is easy to implement, can be pipelined and parallelized, and lets the sender precompute the key stream once the nonce and IV are assigned. The receiver cannot precompute, because the IV is not known until the packet arrives. It also uses only the AES encrypt operation for both directions, so implementations are smaller.

For key sizes, 128 bits is the default and all implementations MUST support it. Support for 192 and 256 bits is optional (MAY). AES uses 10, 12 and 14 rounds for 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, and implementations MUST use those counts.
sections.eli5: AES makes a long strip of scribbles from a secret key and a counter. You mix the strip into your message to hide it, and the other side mixes the same strip in again to reveal it.

sections.title: The ESP Payload
sections.content:
The ESP payload field is the IV followed by the ciphertext, followed by the authentication data. The IV field MUST be eight octets, and the encryptor MUST choose it so the same value is used only once for a given key. Sending the IV in every packet means the receiver can build the key stream even when packets are lost or reordered.

The encrypted payload holds the ciphertext. AES-CTR itself needs no padding, but ESP still requires padding to 32-bit word-align the authentication data, so the padding, Pad Length and Next Header are concatenated with the plaintext before encryption.

Because a forged ciphertext is trivial to build from a valid one, implementations MUST use a non-NULL ESP authentication method. HMAC-SHA-1-96 is named as a likely choice.
sections.eli5: Every packet carries its own little tag that says which scribble strip to use, so the receiver can still unlock packets that arrive late or out of order.

sections.title: The Counter Block
sections.content:
The counter block is 128 bits, built from three pieces. The nonce is 32 bits and is the most significant part. A fresh nonce MUST be assigned for each security association, at its beginning. It need not be secret but MUST be unpredictable before the association starts. The IV is 64 bits. The block counter is the least significant 32 bits, a big-endian integer that starts at one and goes up by one for each further 128 bits of key stream.

With a 32-bit counter, one packet can hold up to (2^32)-1 blocks, which is 68,719,476,720 octets. The RFC notes that this is enough for any IPv6 jumbogram.
sections.eli5: Each scribble strip starts from a three-part ticket: a number picked when the call begins, the packet's own tag, and a counter that ticks up for every piece of the strip.

sections.title: Keys, Nonces and IKE
sections.content:
Fresh keys are required, and the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) can supply them along with the nonce. The requested keying material (KEYMAT) MUST be four octets longer than the AES key. The first part is the key and the last four octets are the nonce. So a 128-bit key needs 20 octets of KEYMAT, a 192-bit key needs 28 and a 256-bit key needs 36. The RFC notes that this way of getting the nonce makes it secret as well as unpredictable.

For IKE Phase 2, IANA has assigned ESP Transform Identifier 13 to AES-CTR with an explicit IV, and the Key Length attribute MUST be present with a value of 128, 192 or 256. The RFC does not define AES-CTR for IKE Phase 1; that would need a separate specification and a new identifier.
sections.eli5: The two sides agree on a fresh secret each time, and four extra bytes of that secret become the starting number for the counter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Used properly, AES-CTR gives strong confidentiality, and the RFC cites analysis showing its privacy guarantees are at least as strong as CBC mode with the same block cipher. But it is very easy to misuse. If a counter block value is ever used for more than one packet under the same key, the same key stream encrypts both packets. XORing the two ciphertexts then cancels the key stream and leaves the two plaintexts XORed together, which is a catastrophic leak. For this reason AES-CTR is inappropriate with static keys, and ESP implementations MUST use fresh keys.

When IKE sets up the keys, separate keys are used for the two traffic directions. If some other mechanism provides one key for both directions, peers will likely pick the same IV values, so implementations that share a key across directions MUST ensure the two peers assign different nonce values.

Forgery is also trivial in CTR mode: an attacker who knows a plaintext can XOR in a chosen change and the receiver will decrypt exactly what the attacker intended. Hence ESP authentication is mandatory.

Finally, AES ciphertext becomes distinguishable from random after 2^64 blocks under one key, so implementations SHOULD generate a fresh key before 2^64 blocks are encrypted. The unpredictable nonce also makes precomputation attacks harder, though long keys are the best defence.
sections.eli5: If you ever reuse a scribble strip, someone can compare two scrambled messages and peel the secret away. So always use a fresh strip, and add a seal so nobody can tamper with the message.

sections.title: Why an Explicit IV
sections.content:
The RFC explains that the ESP sequence number could have served as an implicit IV. It chose an explicit IV field instead, which is not a cryptographic security issue, since both prevent counter block collisions. Reasons given include that only the encryptor can guarantee uniqueness, that implementers may use adders, LFSRs or any other technique, that the decryptor is unaffected by the encryptor's choice, and that a device with several hardware encryption engines can give each its own IV prefix.

It also matters for evaluated cryptographic modules: the counter block assignment needs to be inside the assurance boundary, which is not always true of sequence number assignment. The 64-bit IV overhead is described as acceptable, at about one-third of the overhead of AES-CBC.
sections.eli5: Giving each packet its own tag, instead of reusing the packet's number, lets each sender pick whatever tagging method suits its hardware.
